067:1: When the Planetary Prince rebelled, what kept Van and Amadon steadfast to the end, and what effect has that sin left on us?
067:4: In Paper 66 we saw how the Caligastia one hundred slowly raised primitive mankind at Dalamatia, until all of it was put at risk by the Prince's self-love. Now Paper 67 tells how the rebellion actually came about and what consequences it left behind.
067:5: The problems of human existence on Urantia cannot be properly understood without knowing the great ages of the past, especially the outbreak of the planetary rebellion and its results. This upheaval did not greatly disturb organic evolution, but it markedly changed the course of social evolution and spiritual development and deeply affected the whole superphysical history of the planet (67:0.1).
067:6: How, then, did the rebellion begin, who made what choices, and can another's sin really harm even our eternal destiny?
067:8: Never does the sin of any being rob another of the realization of the divine right of personality survival. (67:7.5)
067:12: When Caligastia had ruled Urantia for three hundred thousand years, Satan, Lucifer's assistant, came on a visit of inspection. He was no hideous figure but a brilliant Lanonandek Son. Satan told of the declaration of liberty Lucifer was preparing, and Caligastia agreed to betray the planet once the rebellion was proclaimed (67:1.1-1.2).
067:13: There is no more sacred trust than that given to a Planetary Prince, and no evil is more destructive of personality than betraying friends who trust and follow. By this deliberate sin Caligastia so completely distorted his personality that his mind never again regained its balance (67:1.3). Here the text distinguishes four stages of wrongdoing (67:1.4-1.5).
067:19: A misconception or distortion of reality
067:22: A partial realization of, or maladjustment to, reality
067:28: Open and persistent defiance of recognized reality
067:31: When sin is repeated it becomes a habit, and the habitual sinner easily falls into iniquity. All sin can be forgiven, but whether a confirmed iniquitous person would ever sincerely feel sorrow or accept forgiveness is doubtful (67:1.6).
067:33: One midwinter Daligastia called together the ten councils and demanded that they give up all their powers, since Caligastia was about to proclaim himself absolute sovereign of Urantia (67:2.1). Van, chairman of the supreme court, declared this an act bordering on planetary rebellion and urged an appeal to Lucifer. But word came from Jerusem to obey Caligastia absolutely, and Van, in a seven-hour address, indicted the three rebels and appealed to Edentia for support (67:2.2).
067:34: At that moment the system circuits were cut, Urantia was completely isolated, and Daligastia proclaimed Caligastia God of Urantia (67:2.3-2.4). Seraphim, cherubim, and even beings who happened to be staying here all had to choose between the way of Lucifer and the will of the Father. This struggle went on for more than seven years, and Edentia did not intervene until everyone had made a final decision (67:2.5-2.6).
067:36: War in heaven broke out on Jerusem and spread to every planet of the system (67:3.1). On Urantia forty of the one hundred, including Van, refused to rebel, but almost half of the administrative and transition seraphim, along with 40,119 primary midwayers, went over to Caligastia (67:3.2). The loyalists, protected by the faithful midwayers, kept the tree of life in an undefended settlement east of Dalamatia (67:3.4-3.5).

067:43: Almost half went over to Lucifer
067:47: Fifty-six loyal (including sixteen attendants of rebel staff members)
067:49: Van's unwavering loyalty was the result of clear thinking, wise reasoning, sincere motives, unselfish purpose, disciplined character, and the unqualified dedication of his personality to the will of the Father (67:3.6). His human associate Amadon, a descendant of Andon and Fonta, did not yield to Daligastia's sophistries throughout those seven years (67:3.8). Caligastia, with the greatest intelligence and experience, went astray, while Amadon, lacking both intelligence and universe experience, stood firm to the end (67:3.9).
067:51: ⟦Q 67:3.9⟧Mind and spirit, when fully united, are potential for the creation of superhuman values, even morontia realities.⟦/Q⟧ (67:3.9)
067:53: Only after the last personality had made its decision did a Most High of Edentia come with the emergency Melchizedeks to take over authority, and the probationary era of planetary rehabilitation began (67:3.10).
067:55: At the final roll call forty of the one hundred were saved, and they later resumed their Paradise journey on Jerusem (67:4.1). Each council chose differently.
067:78: The sixty rebels took Nod as their leader, but they soon lost the system life circuits and fell to mortal existence. At Daligastia's bidding they produced offspring, whose descendants were called the Nodites and whose land was called the land of Nod (67:4.2). The legends of gods coming down to marry with men, and much idol worship, came from this (67:4.3-4.4). The fate of the sixty rebels is not known, and their Adjusters are still waiting on Jerusem (67:4.5). Yet it is believed that many who sincerely repented will in some way be rehabilitated when the adjudication is complete (67:4.7).
067:80: For almost fifty years after the rebellion the whole region of Dalamatia was in great confusion. In the policy of cultural progress, revolution took the place of evolution, and when radical methods were applied to the outlying tribes, liberty quickly turned into license (67:5.1). Because the doctrine of liberty was taught too soon, half-savage tribes overran the city, and the rebel staff were driven north (67:5.2). Society sank back to the old biologic level (67:5.3).
067:81: One hundred and sixty-two years after the rebellion a great tidal wave swept over Dalamatia, and the planetary headquarters sank beneath the sea. By then the apostates who remained there had turned the Father's temple into a shrine to Nog, the false god of light and fire (67:5.4-5.5).
067:83: Van's followers withdrew to the highlands west of India and planned the rebuilding of the world (67:6.1). Van entrusted social administration to ten commissions of four each, and after the loyal staff departed for Jerusem, the Amadonites took over this responsibility (67:6.2). The one hundred and forty-four Amadonites became a biologic leaven, supplying the world with leadership throughout the long dark ages (67:6.3).
067:84: Through the tree of life and the ministry of the Melchizedeks, Van and Amadon lived more than one hundred and fifty thousand years and worked until Adam came (67:6.4). Urantia was governed by a council of twelve Melchizedek receivers, and Van faithfully carried out their policies, founding more than three hundred and fifty advanced groups around the world within less than a thousand years after the rebellion (67:6.5-6.6). Edentia at once upheld Van's appeal, but because the circuits were cut the verdict could not be delivered, and it was found only recently inside the relay energy transmitters (67:6.9).
067:86: The personal consequences of persistently and deliberately rejecting light are solely an individual matter between God and his creature. But the outward repercussions of sin are collective, reaching every being within its sphere of influence (67:7.1-7.2). Fifty thousand years after the planetary administration collapsed, mankind was hardly better off than when Caligastia arrived (67:7.3).
067:91: Individual — a matter between God and his creature
067:93: Collective — reaching every being within its sphere
067:95: Intellectual development, moral growth, social progress
067:97: The individual's spiritual attainment in knowing God and doing his will
067:99: Sin is fatal to personality survival only when it becomes the attitude of the whole being—the choosing of the mind and the willing of the soul (67:7.4). Caligastia rebelled and Adam and Eve defaulted, but no mortal born since has suffered any loss in his personal spiritual experience because of it. In its moral guilt and spiritual consequences, sin is wholly personal (67:7.6-7.7).
067:101: The records of Salvington portray Amadon as the most outstanding figure in all Satania for rejecting the tide of sedition and remaining unswervingly devoted to Van (67:8.1). The Melchizedek who wrote this paper recalls the uplift he felt on Edentia as he listened day by day to the broadcasts of the steadfastness of a once half-savage human being (67:8.2).

067:105: The loyalty of Amadon and his 143 resolute fellows has already done more good in Nebadon and Orvonton than all the evil and sorrow of the Lucifer rebellion combined (67:8.4). And it sheds a glorious light on the wisdom of the Father's plan to gather the corps of mortal finaliters chiefly from ordinary mortals like the indomitable Amadon (67:8.5).
067:107: Paper 67 tells of a rebellion that brought a world to ruin, and at the same time shows the loyalty that shone amid the wreckage. A Prince with the finest intelligence and experience gave himself to self-exaltation and betrayed his trust; as a result Dalamatia sank into the sea and the progress of mankind was long delayed. Yet Amadon, a human being lacking both intelligence and experience, stood unmoved beside Van for seven years, and the whole universe waited for news of him. Sin leaves wide wounds on society and civilization, but its moral guilt and spiritual consequences are wholly personal. No one else's sin, therefore, can stop our choice to know God and do his will.

067:126: An ordinary mortal's loyalty did more good than all the evil of the rebellion
067:129: Another's sin can throw the world into disorder, but one person's choice to be loyal to God can never be broken.
068:1: Civilization is not inborn—so what first drove mankind to begin building it, and how has it been carried on?
068:4: In the preceding papers we saw the missions of the Planetary Prince and of Adam, and Urantia after they miscarried. Now, from Paper 68 on, we turn our eyes to man himself and begin the story of the long, long struggle by which mankind, little better than the animals, came to an imperfect but real civilization (68:0.1).
068:5: This paper starts from one sentence: civilization is a racial acquirement; it is not biologically inherent. The superior traits of civilization—science, philosophy, religion—are not passed on by heredity, so every child must be reared in culture, and each generation must be educated anew (68:0.2). The co-operative social order began with the teachers of Dalamatia, who for three hundred thousand years trained mankind in the idea of group activities (68:0.3).
068:6: What, then, made primitive men, who had no natural liking for one another, band together? And by what is the society thus formed maintained, and by what does it fall?
068:8: ⟦Q 68:2.11⟧Self-maintenance builds society; unbridled self-gratification unfailingly destroys civilization.⟦/Q⟧ (68:2.11)
068:12: Primitive man did not naturally overflow with a spirit of brotherhood. The early races learned only through bitter experience that “⟦Q 68:1.1⟧in union there is strength⟦/Q⟧,” and this lack of a natural brotherly attraction is still an obstacle to the brotherhood of man (68:1.1). Going about alone without a tribal mark was fatal, so civilization became man's insurance against violent death, and the premiums are paid by obedience to the laws of society (68:1.2-1.3).
068:13: Society was born not simply from numbers gathering together but from the organization of intelligent co-operators. Man first learns co-operation through fear and later discovers that it is the most profitable (68:1.4). The earlier a people was organized, the better it survived, and so, despite countless mistakes, civilization has steadily advanced (68:1.5). That is why the text calls the slogan “back to nature” a delusion that believes in a fictitious golden age (68:1.7).
068:15: ⟦Q 68:1.2⟧Civilization has become man's insurance against violent death, while the premiums are paid by submission to society's numerous law demands.⟦/Q⟧ (68:1.2)
068:18: The herd instinct alone cannot explain today's social organization. Man's sociability is largely acquired, and what gathered men together and held them was four great influences (68:2.4). Hunger was so great that history may be called the record of the struggle for food, and putting food by was primitive man's first self-discipline (68:2.5).
068:23: First brought people together — an urge shared with the animals
068:25: Formed the family, but was temporary and spasmodic
068:27: Needing an audience to show off to, it held people together
068:29: Bound society firmly and gave it a superhuman aspect
068:31: Sex urge alone could not get men to shoulder the burdens of family. The early home was built on the sex restlessness of the male and the devoted mother love of the female, and because of the helpless infant, the home was always where the woman was (68:2.6). Nearly all the enduring values of civilization are rooted in the family, and the family was the first successful peace group (68:2.8). Vanity was the origin of art, ceremony, and sport, but the text warns that today pleasure-want has replaced hunger-want, and self-maintenance is degenerating into dangerous self-gratification (68:2.10-2.11).
068:36: Gives birth to society and builds it
068:38: The true purpose of home and marriage (68:2.9)
068:43: If primitive desires gave birth to society, the fear of ghosts held it together. Ordinary fears were physiological, like hunger or pain, but ghost fear was a new and sublime kind of terror (68:3.1). The text names the ghost dream as perhaps the greatest single factor in human social evolution. Animals do not imagine survival after death, so this was one of the earliest differences between the animal mind and the human mind (68:3.2).
068:44: This baseless fear drove loose groups into better-controlled ones and prepared the mind for the later discovery that “⟦Q 149:6.5⟧the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom⟦/Q⟧.” The fears of evolution are designed to be replaced by the awe for Deity inspired by revelation (68:3.3). Yet hunger, love, vanity, and fear alone cannot bear the strains of society to the end, and they finally lead to war. Mankind's peaceful tendencies are not inborn but come from revealed religion, especially the teachings of Jesus, the Prince of Peace (68:3.4-3.5).
068:53: Withstands the strains and promotes peace
068:56: Every modern social institution is an evolution of the primitive customs of our savage ancestors. As the individual has habits, the group has customs, and these grow into folkways and popular conventions (68:4.1). The mores were man's first social institution, arising from the effort to avoid pain and humiliation and to enjoy pleasure and power (68:4.2). The belief that the dead would punish the living who scorned their way of life made the mores firm (68:4.3).
068:57: Before the teachers of Dalamatia, the savage was a slave to the tyranny of custom from morning till night (68:4.4). Yet custom is not wholly evil. Primitive man's inertia was a biologic safety brake that kept him from plunging into too-rapid change, and custom was the thread of continuity that carried civilization along (68:4.5-4.6). No civilization has survived the abandonment of its mores without adopting better ones, and not every change was progress; there were many retrogressions (68:4.6-4.7).
068:62: A tyranny of custom with nothing free or original
068:64: Prevents the maladjustment of too-rapid civilization
068:66: Gradual evolution, rather than radical revolution, keeps civilization alive
068:69: The land is the stage of society, and men are the actors. The evolution of the mores always depends on the ratio of land to men, and land techniques plus standards of living equal the sum of the folkways and mores (68:5.1). The first cultures arose along the rivers of the Eastern Hemisphere, and the march of civilization had four great stages (68:5.2).
068:74: Food-collecting lines driven by hunger — primitive nomadic culture
068:76: The invention of weapon tools freed man from food slavery
068:78: Living on the increase of the herds—the interest on capital
068:80: The domestication of plants — the highest type of material civilization
068:82: Herding gave more leisure but greatly lowered the status of woman. Man, getting his food from his herds, became independent of woman, and the text records that by the end of this age woman was treated almost like a human beast (68:5.7-5.8). Agriculture increased the land-man ratio more than fourfold, and growing plants ennobles every race (68:5.9-5.10). Hunters and herders were warlike, but farmers love peace, and even an industrial age cannot survive unless it stands on a sound agricultural foundation (68:5.11-5.13).
068:84: Man is a creature of the soil; his basic struggle has been, and will always be, for land. The ratio of land to men lies beneath all social civilization (68:6.1). Population is directly proportional to land technique and inversely proportional to the standard of living. When land was plentiful, human life was valued; when land was scarce, the value of life fell (68:6.3).

068:89: Struggle breaks out again, and the worse side of human nature shows
068:90: Better yield, expanding techniques, falling population
068:91: The better side of human nature develops

068:95: Families grow smaller — excessive luxury invites self-destruction
068:97: The text calmly records that the early races relied on practices such as infanticide and abortion to limit their numbers, and that many clans were virtually exterminated as a result. Yet a child once suckled was seldom killed, so strong was the mother's affection (68:6.8-6.9). Finally, the text foresees that as war and disease decline, the population problem will become a test of the wisdom of world leadership, and it explains that the reproduction of normal people, the backbone of civilization, should be encouraged (68:6.11).
068:99: Paper 68 shows that civilization is not something built into man but began when people, driven by hunger and fear, reluctantly banded together. Vanity and ghost fear held that union together; custom became both a bondage and the thread that carried civilization along; and the ratio of land to men lay beneath it all. But as this paper repeatedly stresses, these evolutionary motives alone do not lead to peace. When self-maintenance degenerates into self-gratification, civilization falls, and mankind's peace comes from revelation and the teachings of Jesus. That is why civilization is an inheritance that must be taught anew and guarded anew in every generation.
068:104: Not brotherhood but fear and need first brought people together
068:106: Hunger, sex love, vanity, and fear gathered and held society together
068:108: Ghost fear bound society, but peace comes from revelation

069:1: Out of what fears and needs were today's institutions—industry and trade, capital and property—born, and how should we govern them?
069:4: In Paper 68 we saw how hunger and fear first brought people together, and how custom hardened into the mores and carried civilization along. Paper 69 looks one by one at the institutions that grew from those customs accumulated over long ages. Man surpasses his animal ancestors not only in his ability to appreciate humor, art, and religion but also in being a toolmaker, a communicator, and an institution builder (69:0.1).
069:5: Groups that endure always culminate in institutionalization, and most of those institutions have saved labor and increased group security (69:0.2). Yet every human institution is simply an accumulation of the mores of the past; the heritage preserved by taboos and dignified by religion becomes tradition, and tradition in the end becomes convention (69:0.3).
069:6: Out of what needs, then, did industry and trade, capital and private property grow? And what must we understand if we are to govern our institutions rather than be governed by them?
069:8: ⟦Q 69:1.1⟧Man should control his institutions rather than permit himself to be dominated by these creations of advancing civilization.⟦/Q⟧ (69:1.1)
069:12: Every human institution serves some social need, but when it is overdeveloped it overshadows personality, diminishes initiative, and lowers the worth of the individual. That is why man must control his institutions (69:1.1). The text divides human institutions into three classes, which are closely interwoven and function together as one social mechanism (69:1.2-1.6).
069:19: Industry, property, war for gain, regulative machinery
069:22: The home, the school, education, ethics, religion, marriage customs
069:25: Dress, adornment, war for glory, dancing, games
069:27: It is also worth remembering that fear, ignorance, and superstition played a prominent part in the early origin of every institution, and that civilization has never evolved a clear-cut institution for self-gratification (69:1.3, 1.5).
069:29: Primitive industry grew slowly as an insurance against the terrors of famine. Man learned from the animals that store up food in times of plenty (69:2.1). Poverty is man's natural estate; wealth is not a natural gift but comes from labor, knowledge, and organization (69:2.2). Association led to organization, and organization to the division of labor; what drove the naturally lazy early races into industry was the twofold demand of the struggle for existence and a rising standard of living (69:2.3-2.4).
069:30: Labor—planned effort—distinguishes man from the beast, and the necessity of labor is man's greatest blessing. The Prince's staff worked, and Adam worked in tending the Garden; the Hebrews were the first people to decree, “⟦Q 69:2.5⟧If any man will not work, neither shall he eat⟦/Q⟧” (69:2.5). Primitive man was a born gambler, hoping to get something for nothing, but magic slowly gave way to foresight, self-denial, and industry (69:2.7).
069:32: ⟦Q 69:2.2⟧Wealth is not a natural gift; it results from labor, knowledge, and organization.⟦/Q⟧ (69:2.2)
069:35: The division of labor in primitive society was determined first by natural and then by social circumstances, and the text lists them in five steps (69:3.1). The medicine men were the first specialist class exempted from manual labor, and the smiths who worked metals, competing with them, lost out in the first struggle between science and religion (superstition) and opened the first inns outside the settlements (69:3.5-3.6).

069:42: The old and the crippled made tools and weapons, later irrigation works

069:52: Just as contract marriage followed marriage by capture, barter followed plunder by raiding (69:4.1). The first exchange was silent barter, in which armed traders left goods at a neutral spot, and the women who carried the loads opened the first markets. Goods guarded by a fetish were safe from theft, and the market places later became the first sanctuaries, the “⟦Q 69:4.4⟧cities of refuge⟦/Q⟧” (69:4.2-4.4).

069:65: The text judges that commerce, linked with adventure, gave rise to exploration, discovery, and means of transport, and that by promoting the cross-fertilization of cultures it became a great civilizer (69:4.6-4.8).

The tribe's valiant man was the early banker who kept the group's treasure, so the accumulation of wealth led straight to military organization (69:5.2). The text names eight basic urges that led men to accumulate capital (69:5.3-5.11).

069:88: Man's techniques change, but his temperament changes very little, so the old custom of distributing wealth at festivals to win a name lives on in today's gifts and donations (69:5.13). The text records as fact that, despite the abuses of unfair capitalists, capital is the foundation of modern industrial society, and that thanks to capital and invention the present generation enjoys greater freedom than any before it (69:5.15).
069:90: Primitive society rose by means of fire, animals, slaves, and property (69:6.1). Fire making is the basic invention that in a single leap forever separated man from the animals. Fire guarded the night, encouraged social fellowship in the evening, and also served as a safeguard against ghosts (69:6.2).
069:91: Fire became the first means of being altruistic without loss, since one could give embers to a neighbor without losing one's own. The early home was not a building but the family gathered around the fire (69:6.3). Andon, the discoverer of fire, did not worship it, but his descendants came to regard it as a fetish and moved on to fire worship (69:6.4-6.6). Fire gave rise to cooking, which saved vital energy, and opened the way to metalworking, steam, and electricity (69:6.7-6.8).

069:107: At first the whole animal kingdom was man's enemy. Man ate animals, and later learned to tame them and make them work (69:7.1). Domestication came about by accident, from penning up herds of animals, and when species were found that would breed in captivity, it developed into selective breeding (69:7.2-7.3).
069:108: The dog was the first animal to be domesticated, used for food, hunting, transport, and companionship, and thanks to watchdogs whole clans could sleep at night. The dog's keen sense of smell led to the belief that dogs could see spirits (69:7.4). But after domestication coincided with the Caligastia confusion, many tribes treated women like beasts, and the text calls this one of the darkest chapters in human history (69:7.5).
069:110: Primitive man did not hesitate to enslave his fellows, and woman was the first family slave (69:8.1). The text explains that, compared with the early practice of eating, torturing, or sacrificing captives, slavery was a step beyond massacre and cannibalism (69:8.2-8.3). The herders were the first capitalists, using their herds as capital, and when male captives were bound to the land, serfdom began (69:8.5).
069:111: The text says that slavery was the bridge by which society crossed from chaos and indolence to order, and that it was the beginning of government, but it also makes clear that slavery was oppressive and the gravest of evils, secretly attacking society from within (69:8.6-8.8). The invention of machines made slaves obsolete, yet today a new bondage remains, in which people make themselves slaves of debt through ambition (69:8.9-8.10).

069:118: Leaving slaves and animals behind, back to fire—the inorganic world

069:123: Primitive society was practically communal. Its communism was not a theory but a practical, automatic adjustment that prevented abject poverty and begging, but it encouraged idleness and stifled industry and ambition (69:9.1-9.2). The text explains that it gave way to a higher order because it ran counter to four powerful human tendencies (69:9.2).

Property rights are not absolute but purely social, yet modern government, law, civil rights, and peace have grown up around private property (69:9.17). The present order is not sacred, so change it, the text advises, but make certain you are changing for the better (69:9.18).

069:141: Paper 69 shows that industry and trade, capital and private property, which we take for granted today, all grew up little by little amid hunger and fear, vanity and superstition. Having risen from savagery through fire, animals, and slaves, mankind is now finding new power in machines and the elements of nature. This paper says that no institution is sacred, yet it urges us not to go back to formulas our ancestors discarded, but to move forward slowly, toward the better. Institutions arose to serve man, so man must be not their servant but their master.

070:26: Retaliation against a neighboring tribe that caused a fellow's death

070:112: To guard a valuable “spirit” or trade secrets

070:118: Men's mental and physical inequalities give rise to social classes. 070:123: Sex, age, kinship with the chief
070:127: War and migration, conquest and slavery
070:133: Priest-teachers, ruler-warriors, capitalist-traders, and so on

070:145: Nature gives man no rights at all, only life and a world in which to live it. The greatest gift society gives man is security (70:9.1). Society gradually asserted its rights, and the text lists ten present-day rights (70:9.2-9.12).
070:154: Prevention of personal violence and social disorder
070:156: The institutions of marriage and the family
070:166: Improvement of working conditions and rewards
070:168: So that all activities may be exalted by spiritual motives
070:170: Human rights are not inborn but entirely social; they are the ever-changing “rules of the game” of human competition (70:9.13). The text says that equality is the child not of nature but of civilization, and explains that, while society cannot give everyone the same rights, it can promise to administer the varied rights of each fairly. 070:172: In nature justice is a fiction; nature gives only the inexorable correspondence of effect with cause (70:10.1). 070:187: The mores are law in the making, and once long established they crystallize into precise laws (70:11.1). Law is the codified record of long human experience—public opinion made legal (70:11.6).
070:198: To the elders, later to the courts

The aim of primitive justice was less fairness than the prevention of disorder, yet the state of any civilization can be accurately judged by the thoroughness and fairness of its courts and the integrity of its judges (70:11.14).

Neither rights nor justice were given by nature; they are rules of the game set up by society after long experience. This paper urges us not to glorify war but to find ways of peace that can take over what war has done, and to discover and keep for ourselves a representative government with a balance of power. The ideal government is not handed down from above; people must labor to discover it.

071:60: Freedom without education does more harm

071:122: Today's profit-motivated economics is doomed unless it can be enlarged by service motives. Ruthless competition based on narrow self-interest destroys even what it seeks to preserve, and an exclusive profit motive is incompatible with the teachings of Jesus (71:6.1). 071:177: The co-ordinated functioning of men and women, and the service of women

072:1: How did one nation on a neighboring planet—which suffered rebellion and default just as we did—build an advanced government on the home, education, and service?
072:4: From Paper 68 to Paper 71 we looked in turn at how civilization and institutions, government and the state, have evolved on Urantia. Paper 72 turns our eyes outward for a moment. By special permission, a Melchizedek describes the social, moral, and political life of the most advanced human race living on a not-far-distant planet of the Satania system (72:0.1).
072:5: On this planet, as on Urantia, the Planetary Prince went astray by joining the Lucifer rebellion, the Material Son also defaulted, and the world remains isolated, never having received even a Magisterial Son (72:0.3). Of all the Satania worlds isolated by rebellion, its history is the most like Urantia's, and that is why this rare presentation was permitted (72:0.2).
072:6: Under such unfavorable conditions, then, what kind of government, home life, education, and industry did one continental nation achieve? And what should we learn from it, and what should we look at with discernment?
072:8: ⟦Q 72:11.4⟧They have become civilized to that point where they can vigorously defend civilization without yielding to the temptation to utilize their war powers in aggression.⟦/Q⟧ (72:11.4)
072:12: Despite the unfavorable conditions of the planet as a whole, a very superior civilization is growing up on an isolated continent about the size of Australia. Its population is about 140 million, a mixed race made up chiefly of blue and yellow peoples who get along fairly well together like brothers. The average length of life is ninety years (72:1.1). Thanks to high central mountains and heavy rainfall, water power and irrigation are easy, and with abundant natural resources the nation is self-sustaining, though because of its hostile neighbors it has little foreign trade (72:1.2-1.3).

After that the nation gradually passed over to representative government, and the present republic has now lasted two hundred years (72:1.5).

072:22: Elected by social, political, and philosophic groups
072:24: One hundred veterans of civic service, for life — purely advisory

072:33: The state and regional school systems

073:109: Paper 73 is the story of people in a world darkened by rebellion who, trusting in a Son who had not yet come, tended a garden for decades.
